**Before the appointment**
- Add the appointment date in the Doctor tab. MenoMap shows how ready your summary is and what would make it better informed.
- Choose the most important topics and questions; keep it to just three or four.
- Create a summary of the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**During the appointment**
- Hand over or open the first page for the doctor. This page is designed to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, a heat calendar, and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor uses another language, you can create the summary in that language.

**What this summary is and is not**

This summary compiles what you logged and the data you chose to import from the Health app. It is not a diagnosis and not a complete medical record. Any pattern in the summary is only a look at whether things happen together, not proof of cause. The doctor may ask questions the summary cannot answer, which is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add the new medication with its start date. In a few weeks MenoMap can show the data you logged before and after, which makes the next follow-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the date when 12 consecutive months have passed with no period, when not caused by something else (such as pregnancy, certain medications, or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but anywhere from about 45 to about 55 is common.

**Perimenopause** is the several years before that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can be irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent, or further apart. Many of the changes people think of with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, changed sleep and changed mood, often begin during this time, while periods are still happening. Perimenopause can last a few years or much longer, and it differs from person to person.

**Postmenopause** is the whole time after those 12 months. Some symptoms gradually ease over time; some may continue for many more years.

Menopause can come earlier because of surgery removing the ovaries, some cancer treatments, or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency and you should talk to a doctor.

**Working out which stage you are in** For many people over 45, doctors assess perimenopause or menopause from your history and symptoms. A blood test is not always needed, because hormone levels swing up and down from day to day. Blood tests are usually used when someone is young or when the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do** MenoMap cannot tell which stage you are in. What it can do is keep a truthful record of what you notice: hot flashes, sleep, mood, and treatments, so you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden spread of heat, usually in the face, neck and chest, sometimes followed by flushing, sweating, a fast heartbeat, or feeling chilled. Night sweats are the same symptom occurring during sleep, and can be severe enough to wake you or soak the bedsheets.

These are among the most common changes in the menopause years. Some people have a few and mild; some have several a day so that work and sleep are disturbed. For some they fade within a few years; for others they last much longer.

**What may make them easier to happen** Many people notice patterns involving alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress, or thick bedding. These differ a lot between people, so tracking your own tags may be more useful than a general list.

**Other causes are possible** Flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety, and other conditions. If your symptoms do not look like the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever, or feeling unwell, tell a doctor.

**Describing the symptoms clearly** Details that are useful at an appointment:
- Roughly how many times per day and per night
- How intense it feels and how long it lasts
- What it interferes with: sleep, work, conversation, exercise
- What seems to happen before the symptom
- What you have tried and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's hot flash button and back-logging are there to collect this information without much effort.

**Help is available** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as everyday practices. Which option suits you is something to discuss with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone replacement (often called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen the body makes less of during the menopause years. Major clinical guidelines state it is an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people, and it may help other symptoms too.

**There are several forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as vaginal dryness. People who still have a uterus usually receive a progestogen together with estrogen to protect the uterine lining.

**Benefits and risks depend on the individual:** age, time since periods stopped, personal and family history (such as breast cancer, blood clots, stroke, or heart disease), and the type and way it is used. So this is a decision made together with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app decides.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone replacement an option for me, and why?
- Which type and form does the doctor recommend, and why?
- What might I benefit, and how quickly?
- What are my specific risks, and how do they compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for, and when should we review the treatment?

**If you already use it** record it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap will show your hot flashes before and after you started, to see whether they happen together, not proof. So you have concrete information to discuss when reviewing the treatment.

MenoMap never recommends starting, stopping, or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone replacement is not right for everyone, and some people prefer other approaches, of which there are many.

**Prescription options** Some non-hormonal medicines have evidence of reducing hot flashes: some originally developed to treat other conditions, and a newer class designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has different benefits, side effects, and interactions with other medicines. A doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapy and mind-body approaches** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and helps sleep better. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Adjustments many people find helpful:**
- Layered clothing that comes off quickly
- A fan at the desk and by the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and reducing your own particular triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments can help)
- Regular physical activity and a routine bedtime

**Supplements and herbal products** The evidence for many is inconsistent or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medicines. Tell a doctor or pharmacist about everything you use, including products bought without a prescription.

**Try changing one thing at a time** MenoMap's two-week experiment compares the data you logged yourself before and during the change, which is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most doctor visits are short, and it is hard to recall many nights across the whole month on the spot. People usually remember only the latest or worst day. A simple log helps fill this gap.

**What a daily log gives the doctor:**
- How often and how severe symptoms are, not just that they happen
- Whether symptoms are getting better, worse, or the same
- What happens around the symptoms: sleep, alcohol, stress, medication
- A starting point for comparison, if you try a treatment

**Keep it light** A log only helps if you keep logging. MenoMap is designed with a one-tap hot flash button and a four-question evening check-in, so it takes only a few seconds, no whole notebook needed.

**Two weeks is a good start** Two to four weeks of data usually gives a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and what worries you. MenoMap's Doctor tab helps you choose questions and print them out with your summary.

backTranslations.479:
Once you have had no period for 12 months, **any vaginal bleeding should be examined by a doctor**, even if it happens only once, and even if it is only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time the cause is not serious, such as thinning of the vaginal or uterine lining, which is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat if found early. So public health advice is to get checked rather than wait.

**If you use hormone replacement** some kinds of bleeding may be expected, depending on the type you use. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual, or at the wrong time should also be examined.

**What to do:**
- Contact a doctor or health facility and say that you have bleeding after menopause
- Note the date, amount, and anything else you notice. MenoMap can keep this for you (You → Cycle)

MenoMap cannot say why you are bleeding, but it will remind you to get checked and put this information in your summary for the appointment.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common problems in midlife, and often has more than one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or make you hot or damp so you cannot stay asleep.

**Other common factors:**
- Getting up to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which may help you fall asleep but often makes the second half of the night fragmented
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs, or a bed partner's noise
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which may be a sign of sleep apnea (tell a doctor, especially if you are very sleepy in the daytime)

**What often helps** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layered clothing that comes off; a regular wake time; and less alcohol near bedtime. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied method. Many doctors can direct you to sources of therapy.

**What to track** For one to two weeks, note sleep score, night hot flashes, alcohol, and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and hot flash logging take a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap shows sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside your night sweats, as context, not explanation.

**When to get checked** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (such as driving), mood, or daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping at night.
